He reports significant pain with movement and weight-bearing, and notes the area is swollen. He denies feeling a foreign body upon palpation but reports sharp, localized pain. Last Tetanus shot was 2-3 years ago

instructions: Patient Education: Caring for Your Knee Laceration

You were seen today for a small laceration (cut) caused by glass. You had mild redness, swelling, and discomfort around the injured area.

An X-ray was performed today and did not show any radiopaque foreign body, including visible retained glass, in the soft tissues. Please understand that very small or non-radiopaque foreign material may not always be visible on an X-ray.

Wound Care
Keep the area clean and dry.
Gently wash the wound with soap and clean running water. Avoid aggressive scrubbing.
Apply a thin layer of topical antibiotic ointment as directed.
Cover the area with a clean bandage, particularly while the wound remains open or could become dirty.
Change the bandage at least once daily or whenever it becomes wet or dirty.
Do not pick at or probe the wound.
Pain and Swelling

You may use acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) as needed for pain, if you normally can take these medications safely.

Elevating the injured area when possible may also help reduce swelling.

Watch for Signs of Infection

Return to the clinic or seek medical evaluation if you develop:

Increasing redness, warmth, or swelling
Increasing or severe pain
Pus or other abnormal drainage
Red streaking extending from the wound
Fever or chills
Numbness, tingling, weakness, or difficulty moving the affected area
Persistent sensation that something remains inside the wound
Any worsening or concerning symptoms
Follow-Up

The wound should gradually improve over the next several days. Return for reevaluation if the redness, swelling, or pain worsens rather than improves, or if you continue to feel that a foreign body may be present despite the negative X-ray.
